title.source: Section check: Stories, lives and public memory
title.note: “public memory” as “ký ức chung”, as in the Vietnamese section title; Lesson 14 says “ký ức công chúng”.

intro.source: 10 questions about Lessons 11–15. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.0.question.source: Each Vessantara panel shows a different episode. What is an episode?

questions.0.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Writing on an object is an inscription. An episode is one part of a story. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.0.options.1.text.source: One part of a longer story

questions.0.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 show two episodes from the same story.

questions.0.options.2.text.source: The wood the paint is on

questions.0.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The panels are painted on teak wood. An episode is one part of a story. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.1.question.source: The Thai panels have inscriptions that name donors. What do the inscriptions tell us?

questions.1.options.0.text.source: Who asked for the panels to be made
questions.1.options.0.text.note: “asked for the panels to be made” as “yêu cầu làm ra”, following Lesson 11 (“Đặt làm một tác phẩm nghĩa là yêu cầu nó được làm ra”).

questions.1.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Named donors asked for them, for religious reasons. We know this, even with no names for the painters.

questions.1.options.1.text.source: The names of the painters who made them

questions.1.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The museum has no names for the painters. The inscriptions name the donors. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.1.options.2.text.source: The year when the story first began

questions.1.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The story is much older than the panels. The inscriptions name the donors. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.2.question.source: The workers in The Harvesters are idealised. What does idealised mean?

questions.2.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Bruegel painted it for a rich trader. Idealised means shown as better than real life. Look back at Lesson 12.
questions.2.options.0.feedback.note: “trader” as “thương nhân” (Lesson 12 uses “thương nhân” for the Antwerp merchant).

questions.2.options.1.text.source: Shown just as they really lived

questions.2.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. That is the opposite. Idealised means neater and more perfect than real life. Look back at Lesson 12.

questions.2.options.2.text.source: Shown neater than in real life

questions.2.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. The workers look neater and better than they did in real life. It is one view of farm life.

questions.3.question.source: Why did Millet begin to make prints like The Gleaners?

questions.3.options.0.text.source: Partly to earn money and find buyers

questions.3.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Prints helped Millet reach buyers. Many of them were middle class.

questions.3.options.1.text.source: To copy a painting by Bruegel

questions.3.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Millet's print is his own work, made almost 300 years after Bruegel. Look back at Lesson 12.

questions.3.options.2.text.source: Because a rich patron ordered just one

questions.3.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. A print is made in many copies for many buyers. Millet made prints partly to earn money. Look back at Lesson 12.

questions.4.question.source: What does Monet's painting of Argenteuil show in one picture?
questions.4.question.note: “in one picture” as “trong cùng một bức tranh”.

questions.4.options.0.text.source: A busy city street with no trees

questions.4.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The painting shows a river path with trees and boats. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.4.options.1.text.source: Boats and trees, and factories far off
questions.4.options.1.text.note: “Boats and trees, and factories far off” as “Thuyền, cây, và nhà máy ở xa”.

questions.4.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Fun on the river and factory chimneys share one scene. Nature and people's work are not split apart.

questions.4.options.2.text.source: Farm workers cutting grain in a field

questions.4.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. That is The Harvesters. Argenteuil shows a river town near Paris. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.5.question.source: In The Railway, a woman faces us and a girl looks through a fence. What can a careful viewer say?

questions.5.options.0.text.source: What the two people are thinking

questions.5.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The painting cannot show their thoughts. We can only guess. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.5.options.1.text.source: What they said to each other

questions.5.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. A painting cannot prove a conversation. It is easy to make one up. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.5.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. We can describe what we see, such as where they look. Their thoughts stay unknown.
questions.5.options.2.feedback.note: “Their thoughts stay unknown” as “Suy nghĩ của họ vẫn chưa được biết”.

questions.6.question.source: Rodin shows six citizens side by side, all on one level. What does this choice show?

questions.6.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The town first planned a monument to one man. Rodin showed all six instead. Look back at Lesson 14.

questions.6.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The king is not in the sculpture. It shows six citizens facing a hard choice. Look back at Lesson 14.

questions.6.options.2.text.note: “A shared act of courage” as “Một hành động dũng cảm chung”.

questions.6.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Showing all six made the monument about a shared act. Each man reacts in his own way.

questions.7.stimulus.body.source: This is a made-up example. Bronze statue of a sailor. It remembers a great storm in the year 1650. The artist made the model in 1900. This bronze cast was made from the model in 1990.

questions.7.question.source: When was this bronze statue itself made?

questions.7.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. The model came first. The bronze cast was made much later, in 1990.

questions.7.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The storm is what the statue remembers. The bronze was made long after. Look back at Lesson 14.

questions.7.options.2.text.source: In 1900, when the model was made

questions.7.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The model was made in 1900. The bronze cast came later. Look back at Lesson 14.

questions.8.question.source: In Pieneman's painting, Dutch officers stand high under a raised flag. What does this choice do?

questions.8.options.0.text.source: It shows how Diponegoro felt inside.

questions.8.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. A painted face or pose cannot prove what a person felt. Look back at Lesson 15.

questions.8.options.1.text.source: It makes Dutch power look certain.

questions.8.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. The painting was made for General De Kock. The tall officers and the flag make Dutch power look sure.

questions.8.options.2.text.source: It questions the power of the Dutch.

questions.8.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Saleh's later painting is the one scholars see as a challenge. Look back at Lesson 15.
questions.8.options.2.feedback.note: “scholars” as “các học giả”; Lesson 15 says “các chuyên gia”.

questions.9.stimulus.title.source: Two made-up paintings of one boat race

questions.9.stimulus.body.source: This is a made-up example. A boat race took place in the made-up town of Pellam. The winning captain paid a painter to show the race. Years later, a second painter showed the same race from the losing crew's side.

questions.9.question.source: Which question is most useful to ask about the first painting?

questions.9.options.0.text.source: Who paid for it, and why?

questions.9.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. A commission matters. The captain paid for it, so it may show the race his way.
questions.9.options.0.feedback.note: “A commission” as “Một đơn đặt hàng”, the Lesson 15 glossary word.

questions.9.options.1.text.source: Is it bigger than the other one?

questions.9.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Size does not tell you whose view it shows. Ask who it was made for. Look back at Lesson 15.

questions.9.options.2.text.source: What colour is the captain's coat?

questions.9.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. That is a small detail. Ask who paid for it and why. Look back at Lesson 15.

results.high.source: Well done. You know a lot about how pictures and monuments tell stories and shape memory.

results.middle.source: Good work. You remember many of the main ideas. Look back at any lesson you want to check.

results.low.source: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 11–15, then try again whenever you like.
